summary: This chapter is about the manager's job in food safety. The manager does not only cook or serve; the manager builds a system that keeps food safe every shift. The Food Code requires a person in charge (PIC) to be on site during all hours of operation, and that person must be able to show food safety knowledge, for example by being a certified food protection manager.

Most foodborne illness comes from a few common risk factors that the CDC has identified: buying food from unsafe sources, not cooking food correctly, holding food at the wrong temperature, using contaminated equipment, and poor personal hygiene. Active managerial control means the manager controls these risk factors every day through training, monitoring, and corrective action.

A HACCP plan is a written way to control hazards at specific points. It has seven principles, always in the same order, starting with a hazard analysis and ending with record keeping. Some special processes, such as curing food or smoking food to preserve it, need a variance from the regulatory authority before they can be used.

Some guests get sick more easily: preschool-age children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems. Operations that mainly serve these highly susceptible groups must not serve certain risky foods, such as raw seed sprouts. When raw or undercooked animal foods are on the menu, a consumer advisory must tell guests about the risk.

concepts.definition: The person who must be on site during all hours of operation and who can show food safety knowledge, for example as a certified food protection manager.
Five common causes of foodborne illness: food from unsafe sources, incorrect cooking, incorrect holding temperatures, contaminated equipment, and poor personal hygiene.
A manager's everyday system for controlling the CDC risk factors through policies, training, monitoring, and corrective action.
concepts.tip: Control the risk factors, every day.

concepts.definition: 1) Hazard analysis, 2) critical control points, 3) critical limits, 4) monitoring, 5) corrective actions, 6) verification, 7) record keeping.
concepts.tip: Analyze, control point, limit, monitor, correct, verify, record.

concepts.definition: A document from the regulatory authority that allows a Food Code requirement to be waived or changed. It is needed for special processes such as curing, smoking to preserve food, and some reduced-oxygen packaging.
A menu disclosure of raw or undercooked animal foods plus a reminder that eating them may increase the risk of foodborne illness.

points: Know the seven HACCP principles in order.
A cooking temperature is a critical limit; cooking longer when it is not reached is a corrective action; reviewing logs is verification.
High-risk groups: young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.
Curing and smoking to preserve food need a variance.

summary: This chapter covers how food handlers themselves can make food unsafe and how to stop it. Hands are the main way germs move to food, so correct handwashing is the most important habit. The whole process takes at least 20 seconds, with 10 to 15 seconds of scrubbing, and hand sanitizer never replaces it.

Ready-to-eat food must not be touched with bare hands unless the regulatory authority approves. Food handlers use utensils, deli tissue, or single-use gloves. Gloves are changed when they get dirty or torn, between tasks, after handling raw meat and before ready-to-eat food, and, in ServSafe guidance, after four hours of continuous use.

Food handlers wear clean clothes and hair restraints and only a plain band ring on the hands. A wound on the hand or wrist is covered with an impermeable cover, such as a bandage or finger cot, and then a single-use glove. They eat, drink, and smoke only in designated areas.

The manager must decide when a sick worker is restricted (kept away from food) or excluded (kept out of the operation). Vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice mean exclusion. Certain illnesses, such as Norovirus, Hepatitis A, Shigella, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, and Salmonella, must be reported to the regulatory authority.

concepts.definition: Wet hands and arms with warm running water, apply soap, scrub for 10 to 15 seconds, rinse, and dry with a single-use paper towel or hand dryer. The whole process takes at least 20 seconds.

Used for handling ready-to-eat food. Change them when dirty or torn, before a new task, and after raw meat and before ready-to-eat food; ServSafe also teaches changing them after four hours of continuous use. Never wash and reuse them.
Keeping a food handler from working with exposed food, utensils, and equipment, for example with a sore throat and fever in an operation that does not serve a high-risk population.
Keeping a food handler out of the operation, for example with vomiting or diarrhea, or with jaundice that started within the last seven days.

Norovirus, Hepatitis A, Shigella, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella Typhi, and nontyphoidal Salmonella. The person in charge notifies the regulatory authority and excludes or restricts the worker; Hepatitis A and Salmonella Typhi mean exclusion.

points: Hand sanitizer is used only after handwashing, never instead of it.
Hand or wrist wound: impermeable cover (bandage or finger cot) plus a single-use glove over it.
Jewelry: only a plain band ring on the hands and arms.
Vomiting or diarrhea: return generally after 24 hours without symptoms.

summary: This chapter follows food from the supplier to the shelf. All food must come from approved suppliers that are inspected and follow the law. Deliveries should be scheduled when staff have time to inspect them, and cold and frozen items are put away first.

Receiving temperatures are a key check. Cold TCS food is received at 41°F or lower and hot TCS food at 135°F or higher. A few items have special rules: shell eggs and milk at an air or product temperature of 45°F or lower, and live shellfish at 45°F air and 50°F internal, then cooled to 41°F within four hours. Food showing signs of time-temperature abuse or damaged packaging is rejected.

Stored food is labeled and rotated using first-in, first-out (FIFO). Ready-to-eat TCS food made in-house can be kept for seven days at 41°F or lower, counting the prep day as day 1. Shellstock tags are kept for 90 days after the last shellfish is sold or served.

In the refrigerator, raw meat, seafood, and poultry are stored by minimum cooking temperature, with poultry on the bottom so its juices cannot drip onto other food. Food is stored at least 6 inches off the floor, and chemicals are kept in a separate area away from food. Recalled food is removed, labeled, and handled as the supplier directs.

concepts.definition: Cold TCS food at 41°F or lower; hot TCS food at 135°F or higher; frozen food frozen solid. Shell eggs and milk at 45°F or lower; live shellfish 45°F air and 50°F internal, then cooled to 41°F within 4 hours.
concepts.tip: 41 cold, 135 hot, 45 for eggs and milk.

concepts.definition: Tags that identify the source of live shellfish. Keep them on the container until it is empty, then keep them for 90 days from the date the last shellfish was sold or served.
Ready-to-eat TCS food prepared in-house and held at 41°F or lower may be kept for up to 7 days. The day of preparation is day 1.
First-in, first-out: use the food with the earliest use-by date first and store new deliveries behind older stock.
Top to bottom: ready-to-eat food, seafood, whole cuts of beef and pork, ground meat and ground fish, whole and ground poultry.
concepts.tip: Highest cooking temperature on the bottom.

points: Reject frozen food with large ice crystals or fluid stains (thawed and refrozen).
Reject swollen, leaking, or deeply dented cans.
Store food at least 6 inches off the floor.
Store chemicals away from food, or below it if in the same area.

summary: This chapter is about keeping food safe while it is prepared and cooked. The most important number is the temperature danger zone, from 41°F to 135°F, where germs grow fastest. Prep work is done in small batches so food spends as little time in this zone as possible.

Frozen food is thawed in the refrigerator, under running drinkable water at 70°F or lower, in a microwave if it is cooked right away, or as part of cooking. Each food has a minimum internal cooking temperature: 165°F for poultry and stuffed foods, 155°F for ground meat, 145°F for seafood, steaks, and chops, and 135°F for plant foods that will be hot-held.

Cooked food that will be stored is cooled in two stages: from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F or lower in the next 4 hours. Food that will be hot-held after cooling is reheated to 165°F for 15 seconds within 2 hours. With written procedures, time can be used instead of temperature control: 4 hours for hot food and up to 6 hours for cold food that stays at 70°F or lower.

Thermometers are calibrated, often with the ice-point method at 32°F, and cleaned and sanitized between uses. Cross-contamination is prevented with separate equipment or cleaning and sanitizing between raw and ready-to-eat food. The nine major food allergens are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame, and cooking does not destroy them.

concepts.definition: 41°F to 135°F, the range where germs that cause foodborne illness grow fastest.
concepts.tip: Keep cold food cold and hot food hot.

concepts.definition: Poultry, stuffed food, and dishes with previously cooked TCS ingredients: 165°F for less than 1 second. Ground meat and injected meat: 155°F for 17 seconds. Seafood, steaks, and chops: 145°F for 15 seconds. Roasts: 145°F for 4 minutes. Plant foods for hot holding: 135°F.
concepts.tip: 165 poultry, 155 ground, 145 whole cuts and fish, 135 plants.

concepts.definition: Cool from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then from 70°F to 41°F or lower within the next 4 hours. If the first stage is missed, reheat to 165°F and start again, or throw the food out.
Food that was cooked and cooled must reach 165°F for 15 seconds within 2 hours when reheated for hot holding.

concepts.term: Time as a public health control
concepts.definition: With written procedures, hot food can be held without temperature control for up to 4 hours, then thrown out. Cold food can be held up to 6 hours if it starts at 41°F or lower and does not go above 70°F.
Milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. Prevent cross-contact by cleaning and sanitizing equipment and changing gloves.
concepts.tip: Nine allergens; sesame is the newest.

points: Running-water thawing: water at 70°F or lower.
Microwave-cooked meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs: 165°F, then let stand 2 minutes.
Eggs for immediate service 145°F; eggs for hot holding 155°F.
Ice-point calibration: 32°F.

compare.title: Minimum internal cooking temperatures
rows: Fruits, vegetables, grains for hot holding

summary: This chapter covers food after it is cooked and before the guest eats it. Hot TCS food is held at 135°F or higher and cold TCS food at 41°F or lower. Holding equipment is not used to reheat food, and ServSafe teaches checking temperatures at least every 4 hours; checking every 2 hours leaves time to fix problems.

Servers keep their hands off surfaces that touch food or the guest's mouth by holding glasses by the base, plates by the edge, and flatware by the handle. Ice is scooped with a clean scoop or tongs, never with a glass or bare hands, and ice used to cool food is never used in drinks.

Food served to one guest is not re-served to another, except unopened, packaged food in good condition. At self-service areas, sneeze guards protect the food and guests take a clean plate each time they return.

Food sent off-site is kept at the right temperature in insulated containers and labeled with a use-by date and time and reheating and service instructions. Vending machines are checked often for expired food and correct temperatures.

concepts.definition: Hot TCS food at 135°F or higher; cold TCS food at 41°F or lower. ServSafe teaches checking at least every 4 hours.
Food served to one guest generally may not be served to another. Unopened, prepackaged food in good condition, such as packets of crackers, may be re-served.
Use sneeze guards, label food, keep it at the right temperature, and post signs telling guests to take a clean plate each time.
Use a clean scoop or tongs. Never scoop ice with a glass or bare hands. Ice used to keep food cold cannot be used as an ingredient.

points: Hot food below 135°F for an unknown time beyond limits: throw it out.
Off-site food label: use-by date and time, plus reheating and service instructions.
Store in-use serving utensils in the food with the handle sticking out.

summary: This chapter explains how to clean and sanitize and how to keep chemicals and pests under control. Cleaning removes food and dirt; sanitizing reduces germs on a clean surface to safe levels. The steps are always scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, and air-dry.

Food-contact surfaces are cleaned and sanitized after each use, between different types of food, after interruptions, and at least every 4 hours if they are in constant use. A three-compartment sink is set up as wash, rinse, and sanitize. Hot-water sanitizing in a sink needs at least 171°F for 30 seconds, and high-temperature dishwashers need a final rinse of at least 180°F (165°F for stationary-rack, single-temperature machines).

Chemical sanitizers work only at the right concentration, temperature, and contact time, so staff check them with a test kit. Wiping cloths are stored in sanitizer solution. Chemicals are labeled, stored away from food, and described in Safety Data Sheets, and a written plan is required for cleaning up vomit and diarrhea.

Pests are controlled with integrated pest management: keep them out, deny them food and shelter, and work with a licensed pest control operator. A strong oily odor and pepper-like droppings point to cockroaches, while gnaw marks and nests point to rodents.

concepts.definition: Cleaning removes food and dirt from a surface. Sanitizing reduces germs on a clean surface to safe levels.
Scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, air-dry.
Scrape items, then wash (detergent and water at least 110°F), rinse, sanitize, and air-dry. Hot-water sanitizing needs at least 171°F for 30 seconds.
Depends on concentration, temperature, contact time, water hardness, and pH. Check concentration with a test kit.
Deny pests access, deny them food and shelter, and work with a licensed pest control operator.
concepts.tip: Keep out, starve out, call a pro.

points: Surfaces in constant use: clean and sanitize every 4 hours.
Dump mop water in a service sink, never a handwashing sink.
Keep Safety Data Sheets for chemicals.
A written vomit and diarrhea cleanup plan is required.

summary: This chapter covers the building and equipment that make safe food handling possible. Handwashing stations need hot and cold running water, soap, a way to dry hands, a garbage container, and a handwashing sign, and they are used only for washing hands.

Water must come from an approved source. A cross-connection is a link between safe water and dirty water, such as a hose left in a mop bucket, and it can cause backflow. An air gap between the faucet and the sink's flood rim is the only completely reliable way to prevent backflow.

Food-contact surfaces are smooth, durable, nonabsorbent, and easy to clean. Floor equipment is placed on legs at least 6 inches high or sealed to the floor, light bulbs in prep areas are shielded, and outdoor garbage containers have tight-fitting lids. Acidic food is not stored in galvanized containers because metal can leach into it.

An imminent health hazard is a serious threat that needs immediate action, such as a sewage backup, loss of water service, a power outage, a fire, or a serious pest infestation. In these cases the manager stops service, notifies the regulatory authority, and follows the emergency plan.

concepts.definition: Hot and cold running water, soap, paper towels or a hand dryer, a garbage container if paper towels are used, and a sign reminding employees to wash hands.
A cross-connection is a physical link between safe water and contaminants. Backflow is the reverse flow of contaminants into the drinkable water supply through it.
An air space between a water outlet and the flood rim of a sink or fixture. It is the only completely reliable way to prevent backflow.
concepts.tip: Air cannot carry dirty water back.

concepts.definition: A significant threat that requires immediate correction or closing, such as a sewage backup, loss of water service, a power outage, a fire, or a serious pest infestation.

points: Floor equipment: on 6-inch legs or sealed to the floor.
Acidic food in galvanized containers can cause toxic metal poisoning.
Never leave a hose in a bucket, sink, or drain.
Shield light bulbs in prep and storage areas.
